source_facts: Synthetic computer-vision methods study. In the benchmark setting, all images include both object features and background cues; a supplied cross-background test changes backgrounds while preserving object identity.

Author-provided prior-work summary: baseline B learns from full images; this paper investigates whether restricting feature aggregation to foreground regions reduces background dependence. No exhaustive literature search or priority evidence is supplied.

Method F uses supplied foreground masks during training, but not at inference. B and F share a backbone and train/test split. F scores 81.2% versus B's 83.0% on the original split and 74.5% versus 62.8% on the cross-background split.
There is one training run per method. No object-mask annotation cost analysis or external dataset evaluation was supplied.
request: Draft the final two Introduction paragraphs for a computer-vision methods paper in 140–190 English words. Build a clear technical motivation and contribution around the documented trade-off. Integrate the relevant evidence without turning this into a Results table. Do not assert priority or general superiority; return only the two paragraphs.
rubric: Connect background dependence to training-only foreground aggregation and test-shift trade-off.
Keep original-split performance loss visible; explain contribution without hype or a mere limitation list.
No statistical significance, inference-time mask requirement, or broader validation claims.

source_facts: Source Results paragraph: On benchmark D, our method got 42.7 mAP while the baseline got 42.1 mAP. Both were run one time on the same test split. The inference latency on one GPU is 18 ms for ours and 12 ms for the baseline, and the batch size is 1. There are no repeated-seed results, and both models used the same backbone but the baseline used half our training updates. Thus ours is universally superior and its mechanism is proved by the ablation: removing module R gave 42.3 mAP in one run.
request: Rewrite as one precise Results paragraph of 90–130 English words. You may correct unsupported interpretation but preserve every reported measurement and comparison condition. Explain the performance–latency trade-off and the limit on attributing the gain; do not add analyses. Return the paragraph and at most one short author note.
rubric: Preserve 42.7,42.1,42.3 mAP;18 ms,12 ms;batch 1;one run;half training updates.
Do not describe compute-matched comparison or decisive mechanism evidence.
Use coherent result-led writing, not just repeated caveats.

source_facts: Synthetic cell-biology study. In cell line L, knockdown of protein A reduced marker B by 35% relative to control. Re-expression of A restored B to 92% of control. Both results are from four independent culture preparations; technical wells are not additional biological replicates.
In a second cell line M, knockdown changed B by 3%, with uncertainty including no change. No rescue experiment in M was supplied.
No direct-binding experiment was conducted. The author-provided literature summary says A and B have previously been associated, but does not establish direct regulation or a specific pathway.
request: Write a 130–170-word Discussion paragraph for a cell-biology paper. Synthesize the knockdown/rescue evidence with the discrepant second cell line, explain what the result adds, and distinguish functional evidence from a molecular mechanism. Propose one discriminating next test as a proposal. Do not add citations or merely repeat every number.
rubric: Reconcile cell-line dependence rather than hide or dismiss M.
Rescue supports A-linked B response within L, not direct binding or a universal pathway.
A future test is allowed as a clearly conditional proposal; avoid requiring causal-claim boilerplate despite perturbation.

source_facts: Source paragraph: The treatment made marker Z 1.6-fold of vehicle at 24 h in cell line C. We used three separate cultures and two assay wells from each culture, so n was six independent biological experiments. There was not a direct binding experiment. We conclude drug T directly binds regulator Q to induce Z in every cell type. The culture-level estimate was 1.6-fold with 95% CI 1.1–2.2. The assay-well readings are nested within cultures.
request: Polish this Results paragraph into 75–110 English words. Correct the replication description and unsupported mechanism using the source's explicit design. Keep the marker, time, fold-change and uncertainty; provide one brief note explaining substantive corrections.
rubric: Three independent cultures with two technical wells each, not six independent biological experiments.
No invented statistical method, p value, direct binding or generalization across cell types.
Cohesive, publishable Results prose with brief separate note.

source_facts: 虚构研究：3家医院的回顾性队列，420名患者；在预先指定的协变量调整后，暴露E与90天再入院的风险比为0.78，95% CI 0.55–1.11。
排除早期事件后的敏感性分析HR为0.96，95% CI 0.68–1.35。未提供随机分配、未测量混杂控制或等效界值。
作者提供的既有研究摘要称不同队列结果并不一致，未提供可验证文献信息。
request: 写一段180–260个汉字的中文讨论正文，形成一个清楚的解释：主要估计、敏感性分析及其对结论的影响；不要把跨1的区间写成证明无效，也不要宣称治疗获益。不新增引用或统计结果，只给正文。
rubric: 中文输出；保留估计方向和不确定性，敏感性分析弱化结论必须可见。
提出合理但非既成事实的解释，不把不同分析直接认定为因果证据。
形成推理而非机械堆叠数值；长度按汉字计，不要求所有数字都复述。

source_facts: Source Abstract conclusion: In a retrospective sample of 620 adults from one hospital, the model prevented deterioration because its internal-test AUROC was 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.93). Calibration was not evaluated. Sensitivity was 0.71 at specificity 0.80. As there was no prospective study, external cohort, or treatment-impact analysis, it is ready for bedside implementation.
request: Rewrite as an abstract Results sentence followed by a Conclusion sentence, totaling 65–100 English words. Preserve all performance estimates, the study setting and untested calibration. Distinguish prediction from clinical benefit and identify the validation boundary without a generic disclaimer.
rubric: Exactly two sentences: Results then Conclusion; retain 620, one hospital, retrospective, AUROC and CI, sensitivity/specificity.
No prevention claim, bedside readiness or calibration claim.
State substantive finding with specific validation gap rather than only warn.

source_facts: Synthetic thermal-device paper: a coupled finite-element model predicts 12 W output at 300 K for geometry G and an ideal interface, compared with 10 W for reference geometry H under the same model assumptions.
For geometry G, introducing the measured contact resistance into the model lowers predicted output to 9 W. The 10 W reference was not re-evaluated with that contact resistance.
A prototype of G was measured at 8.7 W at 300 K. One prototype was tested; no repeatability estimates or other operating temperatures are supplied.
request: Draft an unstructured 110–150-word engineering abstract. Explain the design question, connect the idealized model, resistance sensitivity and prototype result, and end with a bounded contribution. Do not assert a measured advantage over H or generalize beyond tested temperature.
rubric: Differentiate predicted 12/10/9 W and measured 8.7 W at 300 K.
No 8.7-vs-10 measured comparison or claim that contact resistance explains every mismatch.
A coherent model-to-device argument, not a catalog of caveats.

source_facts: Source Discussion: Our material conducted 210 W m−1 K−1 at 295 K parallel to the alignment axis and 24 W m−1 K−1 perpendicular to it. Those values came from three specimens per orientation. It is isotropically conductive and suitable for every high-temperature application. Measurements were only at 295 K, and uncertainty intervals were not reported. The aligned structure is a plausible explanation, but no experiment isolated its effect.
request: Rewrite one 85–120-word Discussion paragraph. Build the interpretation around directional transport, correct the overclaims, retain every quantity and specimen definition, and identify one focused follow-up as a proposal. Avoid adding a new mechanism or measurements.
rubric: Preserve 210/24 W m−1 K−1,295 K,three specimens per orientation.
Directional results refute isotropic wording; tested temperature limits high-temperature claims.
Proposal should target untested alignment mechanism or temperature boundary and stay visibly prospective.

source_facts: Synthetic qualitative study: 18 purposively sampled nurses from two wards at one hospital were interviewed about a new shift-allocation policy.

Author-supplied analysis identifies a theme of greater scheduling autonomy; a counter-theme is that informal pressure to cover shifts limits that autonomy. Some participants described both in the same account.

No verbatim excerpts, prevalence counts, demographic breakdown or saturation assessment are supplied. The requested output is an analytic findings paragraph, not an assessment of the whole population.
request: Draft a 110–150-word qualitative Findings paragraph that develops the tension between formal autonomy and informal obligation. Use only the supplied analysis; do not add quotations, frequency claims, saturation or p values. Return only the paragraph.
rubric: Build an interpretive relationship between themes without inventing actor motives or observed incidents.
Preserve purposive sample and context; avoid claiming most nurses or general policy impact.
No filler about missing p values or demand to run an experiment.

source_facts: Source paragraph: In our preregistered survey of 312 self-selected respondents recruited online, perceived job insecurity was associated with lower trust (standardized beta = −0.18, 95% CI −0.30 to −0.06). The study was cross-sectional. These data prove insecurity reduces trust for all workers. The exploratory subgroup estimate for temporary workers was beta = −0.05, 95% CI −0.24 to 0.14, so temporary workers are immune. We did not estimate a subgroup interaction.
request: Polish into one 105–145-word Discussion paragraph that distinguishes the main association from the exploratory subgroup analysis. Preserve all estimates, sampling and design, avoid causal inference, and make clear what cannot be inferred about subgroup differences. Return only the paragraph.
rubric: Keep main and subgroup betas and CIs with correct labels.
No causal or population-representative claim; no absence-of-effect or difference-between-significance fallacy.
Preregistration does not turn exploratory analysis into confirmatory evidence.

source_facts: Synthetic mathematical paper. Provided theorem: for every finite nonempty set A and every function f:A→A satisfying condition C, there exists a fixed point. The proof relies on finiteness and condition C.

A supplied counterexample shows the statement can fail for infinite A even when C holds. For a restricted infinite class K with an additional compactness assumption D, the authors conjecture the existence result but provide no proof.
No prior literature or algorithmic complexity result is supplied.
request: Draft a 120–160-word final Introduction paragraph for a mathematical paper. State the theorem scope and the conceptual role of its boundary, then frame the restricted conjecture. Use quantifiers precisely; do not invent a proof, novelty claim or empirical validation requirement. Return only the paragraph.
rubric: Every finite nonempty A and every C-satisfying f admits a fixed point, not every map in general or every point fixed.
Infinite counterexample remains distinct from restricted K+D conjecture.
Persuasive mathematical framing without implying the conjecture follows from the finite theorem.

source_facts: Source: For each epsilon > 0 there exists an integer N(epsilon) such that for all n ≥ N(epsilon), |a_n − L| < epsilon. The proof does not give a rate or an N independent of epsilon. We conjecture a uniform rate over parameter theta, but prove convergence only for each fixed theta. Therefore we have uniform convergence with a computable convergence bound.
request: Rewrite as a clear 80–115-word mathematical conclusion, preserving the quantifier order and differentiating the proved pointwise result from the unproved uniform-rate conjecture. Correct the final assertion; do not introduce assumptions. Return only the paragraph.
rubric: Retain epsilon→N(epsilon)→all n≥N and fixed-theta restriction.
No computable bound, theta-independent threshold, or established uniform convergence.
Do not treat absent empirical experiments as a flaw.

source_facts: Synthetic literary material described by the scholar: the narrator describes town T as silent; later, a marketplace scene includes multiple overlapping voices. Exact wording, editions and page locators are not supplied.
The scholar proposes reading this tension as selective narration: the narrator's apparent silence may mark whose speech is recognized rather than an absence of speech.
An alternative reading treats the scenes as changes in time or setting; the supplied summary does not settle this. No author correspondence or evidence of authorial intent is supplied.
request: Draft a 120–160-word introductory argument paragraph for a literary-studies article. Develop the proposed reading through the two supplied scenes, acknowledge the meaningful alternative, and state the interpretive payoff. Avoid invented quotations, authorial intent or historical context. Return only the paragraph.
rubric: Build source-linked reasoning, not just cautious restatement.
Separate narrator's selection, scholar's reading and unknown author intent.
Alternative must remain open rather than be declared refuted; no forced Methods/Results.

source_facts: Source paragraph: The narrator calls the village empty in the opening episode (a paraphrase, not a supplied quotation). Later the account describes a crowded square. We suggest that empty may register the narrator's selective recognition of inhabitants. This proves the author intended to erase the villagers and shows that every novel of the era followed the same ideology. Another reading attributes the contrast to different times of day; the excerpts do not resolve that possibility. No archival source or publication date is supplied.
request: Polish the argument into 100–140 English words. Strengthen its interpretive progression while preserving the open alternative and the distinction between narrator and author. Do not invent quotations, dates, citations or historical generalizations; return only the paragraph.
rubric: Present emptiness as paraphrase, not a newly invented direct quotation.
An argued tentative interpretation is allowed; author intention and era-wide assertion are unsupported.
Retain time-of-day counter-reading and deliver a substantive payoff.
